title: Lateral Movement
summary: Lateral Movement is the tactic describing how an adversary moves between systems inside a network, using stolen credentials, remote management protocols, and trusted administrative channels to reach higher-value targets. Behaviours include remote desktop sessions, server message block and administrative share access, secure shell logins, remote service creation and scheduled task deployment, execution framework agents, and pivoting through compromised hosts to reach network segments that are not directly accessible. The telemetry picture is mixed. Authentication events across directory services and endpoints record the source, target, account, and logon type for most remote access, and service creation, remote process start, and file writes to administrative shares show what the adversary did on arrival. Network flow data identifies new host-to-host relationships and unusual internal fan-out. The core detection problem is that lateral movement is largely indistinguishable from normal administration by design: administrators use exactly these protocols and credentials. What separates them is context, such as an account authenticating from a workstation it never uses, administrative protocols appearing on endpoints where they were previously absent, or a single source touching many targets in sequence. Detection therefore relies on relationship baselines, careful use of honeypot or decoy credentials, segmentation that limits what is reachable, and rapid correlation of authentication, process, and flow evidence into a movement path rather than a list of isolated alerts.
objectives: Describe the remote access protocols and administrative mechanisms adversaries use to move between systems and what each leaves behind.
Correlate authentication, process creation, service installation, and network flow data into a coherent movement path.
Baseline legitimate host-to-host and account-to-host relationships so unexpected pairings become detectable.
Explain how network segmentation and just-in-time administrative access change what lateral movement is even possible.
Use decoy credentials and canary hosts to raise detection confidence without adding analyst load.
Prioritise containment actions that break a movement path rather than only cleaning individual hosts.

beginner.definition: Lateral movement is how an attacker travels from one computer to another inside your network. They rarely break in twice. Instead they reuse stolen credentials and trusted administration tools. The aim is to reach more valuable systems, step by step, while looking like ordinary remote work.
beginner.whyItMatters: One infected laptop is inconvenient. Attackers who move freely can reach your servers, your backups and your most powerful accounts. The problem is that administrators use these same tools every day. You cannot simply block remote access. You need a baseline of who normally connects where, so unusual pairings stand out quickly.
howItWorks: The attacker collects usernames and passwords from the first machine they control.
They try those credentials against other computers, using normal remote access tools.
A successful login gives them a new machine, closer to the systems that matter.
They repeat the process, sometimes using one machine to reach a network segment they cannot see.
Defenders spot this by joining login records, process events and network flows into one path.
beginner.example: Think of a large office where every desk phone can call every other desk. An intruder who learns one extension can ring a colleague and ask to be let into their floor. From there they ring someone else, and each call sounds completely ordinary. Nobody hears anything strange, because phones ring all day. What stands out is the pattern. One person calling twenty different floors in ten minutes is not normal business.
takeaways: Lateral movement is an attacker hopping between machines you already trust.
Stolen credentials do most of the traveling, not clever exploits.
Know which accounts normally connect to which systems, and alert on the rest.
